name: csound
why: A decades-old sound synthesis language where you write orchestras and scores, a deep instrument-building environment that rewards exploration.

brief.what_it_is: Csound is a sound and music computing system, a free and open source audio programming language. You write an orchestra (instrument definitions) and a score (note and control events) as text, and Csound renders them to audio. The homepage says it runs on desktop, mobile, embedded, server and web platforms. The core is a C library with a command-line frontend, plus language bindings and utilities such as csanalyze, pvanal, sndinfo and makecsd. The brew formula lists about 30 executables, including the csound binary itself.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Csound as descended from the earliest computer music software, the MUSIC-N series by Max Mathews, and says it was first released in 1985 by Barry Vercoe. The project describes itself as having been part of the computer music world since then, powering music software and music-making for musicians around the world.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal mechanism. From the repository description, Csound is a core library with a command-line interface, and ports exist for embedded, mobile and web targets. The brew caveats show that Java bindings are shipped as a csnd6.jar and a native shared library.
brief.install_notes: The brew caveats say that to use the Java bindings you may need to add a CLASSPATH export to your shell profile, pointing at $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/csound/libexec/csnd6.jar, and to link lib_jcsound6.jnilib into ~/Library/Java/Extensions. The README points to BUILD.md for building from source on various platforms and to platform/dockerfiles/ReadMe.md for Docker recipes. The homepage offers a Web IDE for trying Csound 7 without installing it. I did not open BUILD.md.
brief.standout: It is one of the oldest continuously developed music synthesis languages, with a lineage going back to MUSIC-N. The scout note describes it as a deep instrument-building environment that rewards exploration, but I did not verify that from the README. The repository's own README says little about features; the depth is in the docs.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub repository's develop branch is the Csound 7.x line, labelled 7.0.0 (beta), with a GitHub Actions build badge and beta installers for macOS, iOS and Windows. The README says the 6.x line is EOL and no more releases are planned. The copyright line runs to 1991-2024. I did not find a last-release date or last-commit date, so the exact activity level is unknown.
brief.caveats: Csound 7 is a beta, and the README calls the develop branch the 7.x line. Csound 6.x is end-of-life, so anyone on the master branch is on the final 6.x release. The code is LGPL 2.1 or later. The Java-binding setup in the brew caveats is macOS-specific (the .jnilib file and ~/Library/Java/Extensions). The README says nothing about installation-time pain, so I can't judge that.

judge.reason: Csound turns text-defined instruments and scores into sound, opening a deep, unusual world of programmable synthesis with roots in early computer music.

entry.title: Csound
entry.tldr: A sound synthesis language from 1985 where you write instruments and a score as text, and the computer renders them into audio.
entry.deeper_look:
Csound is a free and open source audio programming language. You describe instruments in an orchestra, which is code that defines how a sound is built, and you describe what they play in a score, which is a list of note and control events. Csound reads both and renders audio. The core is a C library with a command-line frontend, and the project says it runs on desktop, mobile, embedded, server and web platforms.

It descends from the MUSIC-N series by Max Mathews, the earliest computer music software. In the homepage's words, it "has its roots in the earliest of computer software." Barry Vercoe first released Csound in 1985, and it has been part of the computer music world since then.

The idea underneath is that a sound is a program. Instead of tweaking knobs on a synth, you build the signal path yourself and decide what each part does. That makes it a door into synthesis, signal processing and algorithmic composition. The Homebrew formula installs about thirty executables, including analysis and conversion utilities such as pvanal, sndinfo, csanalyze and makecsd.

The README says little about features. The depth is in the reference manual, so expect to spend your first session reading docs rather than running examples.
entry.install:
brew install csound
# Optional, macOS only, for the Java bindings: add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.profile
export CLASSPATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/csound/libexec/csnd6.jar:."
mkdir -p ~/Library/Java/Extensions
ln -s "$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/csound/libexec/lib_jcsound6.jnilib" ~/Library/Java/Extensions

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options for the renderer, a first look at how orchestra and score files get turned into audio.

entry.whats_unique: It is one of the oldest continuously developed music synthesis languages, with a direct line back to MUSIC-N. Few tools let you build every part of a sound from text.
entry.caveats: Csound 7 is still in beta and the 6.x line is end-of-life, so the Homebrew version and the current docs may not match exactly.
